title: Emerging El Niño effect on Sri Lanka: Be ready for catastrophe | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 04:10
-     - 5

A prolonged El Niño drought forces a massive, unbudgeted outflow of foreign currency to fund these fuel imports. At the same time, because domestic agriculture will be crippled by climate whiplash, the country will be forced to spend even more foreign exchange to import essential foods like rice, milk powder, and lentils just to prevent widespread malnutrition. This creates a worst-case scenario for our Balance of Payments, where our import expenses skyrocket while our agricultural export revenues (such as tea and rubber) collapse due to weather stress. This foreign exchange drain comes at the worst possible moment in our economic history

Chilling warning

The British Meteorological Office has issued a chilling warning that should instantly shake us out of our collective complacency.

According to their latest global climate projections, the planet is on track for a severe El Niño trajectory building toward 2027, which is estimated to be the hottest year of the century1. Alarmingly, scientists warn that this atmospheric disruption could mirror the catastrophic global climate shift of 1877—a dark year in human history when intense global droughts caused absolute crop failures, leading to the starvation and deaths of millions of people across Asia, including neighboring India2.

Ceylon, the name given to it before it became Sri Lanka in 1972, was not affected directly by the disaster, but indirectly through the influx of famished South Indians who were welcome by the colonial planters without regard for cholera and smallpox which they brought to the island3.

The scientific backing behind the Met Office’s warning relies on sophisticated computer modeling of ocean temperatures and satellite tracking. These tools show an unprecedented accumulation of thermal energy in our oceans. When the atmosphere absorbs this heat, it warps global weather systems like a spinning top thrown out of balance. Because our planet’s climate is interconnected, a spike in heat in one ocean triggers a domino effect across the globe. For an island nation like Sri Lanka, still recovering from profound economic vulnerabilities, this warning is not a distant scientific theory; it is a clear and present danger to our food security, power grid, and national financial survival.

Fan and bathtub: Understanding El Niño and La Niña

To understand this global threat, we must understand what El Niño is. Imagine a giant bathtub representing the Pacific Ocean. Normally, a powerful electric fan—representing the steady atmospheric “trade winds”, so called because early sailors used these winds to navigate across oceans, blows across the water from East to West. This fan pushes the warm surface water away from the West side of South America and piles it up over South Asia and Australia. As the warm water moves West, cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the deep ocean floor near Peru to fill the gap.

Centuries ago, Peruvian fishermen noticed that every few years, around Christmas time, this cold water would mysteriously disappear, replaced by an unusually warm ocean current that killed off their fish catches. Because it happened around the birth of Christ, they named this warm current “El Niño,” which is Spanish for “The Boy Child.”

Sometimes, the opposite happens. The cosmic fan blows much harder than usual, piling up even more warm water in the West and making the waters near Peru icy cold. Scientists, and not Peruvians, needing a name for it started calling this cold phase "La Niña" or “The Girl Child”, the exact opposite to El Niño.

Right now, the fan is breaking down. The trade winds are stalling, and during an El Niño year, that massive pile of hot water in the West sloshes backward toward South America. This shifts the entire planet›s rain clouds, bringing floods to desert regions and throwing a blanket of drought over South and Southeast Asia.

Sri Lanka’s impending climate whiplash

How does a shifting ocean current thousands of miles away harm Sri Lanka? It happens through a massive atmospheric highway called the Walker Circulation, named after Gilbert Walker, a Cambridge mathematician who became the head of the Indian Observatories in 1904.

When the Pacific Ocean’s heat engine moves East, it completely alters the air pressure across the Indian Ocean, destabilising its predictable, bimodal monsoon patterns, known as Indian Ocean Dipole or IOD, the difference between the surface sea temperature in the East side, say Indonesia, and the West side, say, East Africa. The current El Niño is expected to activate the positive phase of IOD, raising the temperature on the Western side of the Indian Ocean close to East Africa.

Sri Lanka, though located in the middle, is expected to experience changes in the Monsoon patterns altering rain and drought conditions. This is not good news for its agriculture, both food crops and commercial plantations4.

As Sri Lanka looks toward a potentially record-breaking hot year, Sri Lanka faces what meteorologists call a double-edged sword of agricultural disruptions, striking different regions during different seasons: In the Western and Central zones, El Niño in the Pacific will fail the South-West Monsoon causing severe drought and threatening the current Yala crop. This is currently happening. In the Northern and Eastern zones, there will be flash floods threatening the oncoming Maha crops.

This is the possibility about which Sri Lanka should be adequately wary.

Because El Niño is a global phenomenon, major food-exporting giants like India, Vietnam, Thailand, and Australia will simultaneously battle their own severe droughts, blistering heatwaves, and collapsing crop yields. When global agricultural supply drops, international market prices will skyrocket. Furthermore, exporting nations will look out for themselves first; they will ban international food exports to prioritise feeding their own citizens. This is the usual practice of India which is Sri Lanka’s main food source in an emergency

Power grid crisis: Drying reservoirs and hydropower failure

The agricultural fallout is only one side of the coin; the impending El Niño threatens to paralyse Sri Lanka’s national electricity grid. Sri Lanka relies heavily on its large hydroelectric complexes—such as the Laxapana, Mahaweli, and Samanala reservoir networks—to generate roughly one-third of its domestic electricity. Hydropower is a highly cost-effective, domestic source of clean energy, but it is entirely dependent on consistent monsoonal inflow. A dry spell will cripple hydropower generation forcing CEB to switch to thermal power that needs the country to spend its foreign exchange resources to meet the high energy bills.

When the reservoir water levels plunge drastically, Sri Lanka will be forced to make an impossible choice. It must choose between power generation and food production. Both are important policy goals and in the past, when the country could not afford to use the reservoir waters anymore, it had to generate thermal power to keep factories running. It causes a double whammy: to import food, it should now spend more foreign exchange. Further, thermal power is more expensive and, when CEB adjusts its fares to match the costs, the economy will have to take the additional burden of high costs of production.

Foreign exchange trap: Threat to debt repayment

Relying heavily on fossil-fuel thermal plants to survive a drought creates a direct macroeconomic emergency. Sri Lanka does not produce coal or petroleum; every metric ton used to generate emergency electricity must be purchased from foreign markets using precious United States dollars.

A prolonged El Niño drought forces a massive, unbudgeted outflow of foreign currency to fund these fuel imports. At the same time, because domestic agriculture will be crippled by climate whiplash, the country will be forced to spend even more foreign exchange to import essential foods like rice, milk powder, and lentils just to prevent widespread malnutrition. This creates a worst-case scenario for our Balance of Payments (BOP), where our import expenses skyrocket while our agricultural export revenues (such as tea and rubber) collapse due to weather stress.

This foreign exchange drain comes at the worst possible moment in our economic history. Following our historic sovereign debt restructuring, Sri Lanka has negotiated a grace period on bilateral and commercial debt repayments that shields our economy. However, this safety net is temporary. Principal and restructured interest payments are scheduled to resume in earnest, forcing Sri Lanka to meet heavy international debt obligations.

This will also exacerbate the current foreign exchange crisis. To prevent another devastating economic default, the Central Bank must build and maintain foreign exchange reserves of at least $ 15 billion. If the country wastes its thin, hard-earned dollar reserves—which currently hover precariously under $ 7 billion—on emergency diesel imports and food shipments, it will completely hollow out the existing fragile foreign exchange buffer. The El Niño climate crisis could trigger a secondary economic crisis, breaking Sri Lanka’s post-restructuring financial recovery before it can fully take root.

El Niño is an inevitable force of nature, but our vulnerability to it is entirely man-made. Since we cannot change the winds, we must aggressively change our strategies. The solution lies in proactive human planning, policy mobilisation, and a total rethinking of our resource management

Global food supply squeeze

In past domestic agricultural crises, Sri Lanka simply relied on importing cheap grain from regional neighbours to bridge local food deficits. This time, that exit strategy is off the table.

Because El Niño is a global phenomenon, major food-exporting giants like India, Vietnam, Thailand, and Australia will simultaneously battle their own severe droughts, blistering heatwaves, and collapsing crop yields. When global agricultural supply drops, international market prices will skyrocket. Furthermore, exporting nations will look out for themselves first; they will ban international food exports to prioritise feeding their own citizens. This is the usual practice of India which is Sri Lanka’s main food source in an emergency.

If Sri Lanka waits passively without an immediate plan, it will become helpless victims of a global food shortage. The country cannot import food that isn’t available on the market, and it cannot afford food that is priced in exorbitant, inflated foreign currency.

Man-driven strategies: What we must do right now

El Niño is an inevitable force of nature, but our vulnerability to it is entirely man-made. Since we cannot change the winds, we must aggressively change our strategies. The solution lies in proactive human planning, policy mobilisation, and a total rethinking of our resource management:

Call for an immediate national task force

We cannot afford to treat this incoming crisis with the typical, slow-moving bureaucratic response. If we wait for the reservoirs to run dry and the crops to wither before we act, the economic damage will be irreversible.

The Government must immediately set up a high-level, multi-sectoral National El Niño Response Task Force. This body must bring together the Agriculture Ministry, the Ceylon Electricity Board, the Department of Meteorology, the Irrigation Department, and the Finance Ministry under a unified command structure. To ensure we pass through this period successfully, the task force should be given the legal mandate to execute three highly specialised, non-traditional strategies:

1. Implement a national water credit scheme

Water conservation can no longer rely solely on moral appeals; it must be driven by economic incentives. The Task Force must establish a national water credit scheme targeting the commercial, industrial, and agricultural sectors. Under this framework, large factories, beverage plants, commercial farms, and urban housing complexes will be assigned strict, seasonal water-use quotas.

Entities that consume less than their designated allocation will earn tradable «Water Credits,» which can be sold back to the Government or exchanged for tax deductions. Conversely, those who exceed their limits will face heavy financial penalties. At the village level, the scheme will reward Agricola farmer organisations that efficiently pool canal allocations, transforming water from a neglected public utility into a highly valued national asset.

2. Deploy advanced technology and cloud-seeding partnerships

We must actively mobilise global scientific expertise to fortify our domestic defence. The task force must forge immediate bilateral agreements with international climatology panels and advanced meteorological networks in countries like Australia and Japan. Through these partnerships, Sri Lanka can secure real-time satellite data and predictive AI modelling to monitor localised soil moisture depletion levels.

Furthermore, the Government must prepare frameworks for targeted cloud-seeding operations. By collaborating with seasoned international aviators and environmental scientists, Sri Lanka can deploy aircraft to seed clouds over critical highland catchment areas like Victoria, Castlereigh, and Maussakelle. While cloud-seeding cannot stop a global El Niño, triggering rainfall directly over our primary hydroelectric dams can stabilise our power grid and prevent costly thermal fuel imports.

3. Establish community-level grain and tuber banks

To protect our rural populations from immediate starvation and regional supply lines from collapsing, the task force must decentralise food security. Rather than keeping all buffer stocks in centralised urban silos, the State should utilise our network of Grama Niladhari (GN) divisions to build community-managed grain and tuber banks.

As farmers harvest hardy alternatives like Kurakkan, sorghum, and green gram, the Government will buy these crops at guaranteed baseline prices and store them directly within local rural centres. Communities will also be trained to systematically slice, dry, and preserve cassava harvests into long-lasting flour stocks. If the central distribution networks are broken by fuel shortages or hyperinflation, these decentralised village banks will serve as localised lifeboats, ensuring that every village has enough dry food to survive the peak of the drought.

The countdown to a challenging climate cycle has already begun. The solution lies entirely in proactive human planning, robust policy mobilisation, and swift Government action. We must start preparing our fields, our reservoirs, and our national financial defences today, or prepare to face the consequences tomorrow

Final call to action

Nature has given us a clear warning through the global scientific community. The countdown to a challenging climate cycle has already begun. The solution lies entirely in proactive human planning, robust policy mobilisation, and swift Government action. We must start preparing our fields, our reservoirs, and our national financial defences today, or prepare to face the consequences tomorrow.

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com)

title: Is the request to remand Namal Rajapaksa for 14 days justified? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 04:02
-     - 1

MP Namal Rajapaksa (centre) minutes before boarding the prison bus following the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court order that he be remanded until 18 September after he was arrested by the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption over allegations that he received Rs. 100 million in bribes linked to an aircraft procurement deal involving SriLankan Airlines

An arrest has been made, but indictments have not yet been served. Now the priority must be the expediting of the case. Whatever the decision is, it will be appealed. Hopefully, a final decision can be reached before election season begins in 2028-2029

Given what I had written about the remanding of other politicians, it is reasonable to ask for my response to the above question. Also, I have been pursuing this matter since 2020 when the evidence first emerged.

On 2 January 2024, in an article entitled “What can (and cannot) be done about corruption,” I wrote:

Even more importantly, all who want to live in a decent society under the rule of law must pressure the government to accelerate the complete implementation of the Anti-Corruption Act. With or without all the components being in place, it is important to expedite a case such as that against the former CEO of SriLankan Airlines and his wife, where the relevant evidence is an “agreed Statement of Facts in relation to a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (“DPA”) about the alleged commission by Airbus SE of offences of failure to prevent bribery.” By this means, it will be possible to demonstrate to the public that effective action can be taken against grand corruption without violating legal norms.

Timeline

The admitted payments made to facilitate aircraft and VIP kit purchases by the State-owned airline constituted grand corruption. And the investigation has taken too long. The money changed hands in 2013-2014. I do not say “allegedly” because the evidence includes a UK court document, the Deferred Prosecution Agreement referred to above that includes the following admissions in paragraph 43:

In 2013, Airbus engaged the wife of a person concerned with the purchase of aircraft from SLA through a straw company (the Company of Intermediary 1). Pursuant to the engagement, Airbus employees offered up to $16.84 million to the Company of Intermediary 1 to influence SLA’s purchase of 10 Airbus aircraft and the lease of an additional 4 aircraft. In fact, only $ 2 million of the $ 16.84 million was paid. The Company of Intermediary 1 was approved by Airbus employees as a BP [Business Partner].

The DPA was released in final form on 31 January 2020. Investigations were initiated, leading to the arrest of Kapila Chandrasena [intermediary 1] and his wife in February 2020. Both Chandrasena and his wife were released on bail in March 2020. Not much happened with the investigation during the terms of Presidents Gotabaya Rajapaksa and Wickremesinghe, other than the adoption of the Anti-Corruption Act and the appointment of the current members of CIABOC which were done by the latter.

My article “Other people’s money: Lessons from the Airbus corruption case,” was published on 11 February 2020, a few days after Chandrasena and wife surrendered to the CID, during the term of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa.  

The new, much stronger, Anti-Corruption Act, No. 9 of 2023, was certified by the Speaker on 8 August 2023 at the midpoint of President Wickremesinghe’s term. It was reasonable to plead again for action on this case in January 2024 as the new Members of CIABOC appointed by President Wickremesinghe assumed office. But the Director General position was vacant at that time. That appointment was made by President Dissanayake on 10 January 2025, 20 months ago.

Was 20 months needed to find what happened to the $ 2 million mentioned in the DPA? We should all be pleased that the investigations appear to be complete.

Is the remand request justified?

One justification for remanding suspects is to avoid interference with witnesses and the investigation. Six years and seven months from the initial arrest of Chandrasena and his wife appears more than enough time for whatever interference that was feared to occur. If there is anything that could happen within these 14 days in August 2026 beyond what has happened since 2020, CIABOC could at least give us a hint. Intermediary 1 is dead; his wife, whose company received the bribe, is absconding. A key witness is in Australia, immune to interference.

In the absence of reasons being provided, it is not unreasonable to conclude that the request supported by a certificate from the Director General under section 149 of the Anti-Corruption Act for remanding is performative. Now that the political objective has been achieved, Rajapaksa should be released on bail as soon as possible. The new DG has been in office for 20 months which is plenty to assemble the evidence for this kind of case, especially because the DPA serves as the foundation. 

An arrest has been made, but indictments have not yet been served. Now the priority must be the expediting of the case. Whatever the decision is, it will be appealed. Hopefully, a final decision can be reached before election season begins in 2028-2029.

title: Personal Income Taxation – A growing burden for Sri Lankans and economy | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:59
-     - 3

Sri Lankan resident citizens have to pay tax on interest income which could go up to 36%, whereas on the other hand, non-resident Sri Lankan citizens on the same source of Sri Lankan Rupees are taxed at the rate of 10%. Unless we have a fair and justifiable tax regime, the future is going to be bleak for Sri Lanka

By Cecilia Page

Sri Lanka’s economy has been adversely impacted due to the brain drain of doctors, engineers, university professors, white collar and skilled workers. All major sectors such as health, tourism, education, construction, information technology and the financial sector have been impacted. The brain drain has resulted in appointing foreign nationals to fill these gaps, and if this continues it would have a devastating impact on the economy.

All citizens are entitled to have a reasonable tax-free income and sustainable tax rates and slabs. It is a fact that the cause of the brain drain is due to the high taxes which most of the taxpayers are not in a position to pay. In addition, the Sri Lankan resident citizens have to pay tax on interest income which could go up to 36% whereas on the other hand, non-resident Sri Lankan citizens on the same source of Sri Lanka Rupees are taxed at the rate of 10%, which is a final tax for them.

Due to this loophole, large Sri Lankan deposit holders have been advised to transfer large portions of their deposits to their spouse/children who become non-residents and be entitled to the 10% final tax. This is incredibly unfair to the citizens who remain and serve their country.

Interest income for both resident and non-resident Sri Lankan citizens should be taxed at the same rate of 10% and the tax should be final.

How can lower- and middle-income earners be expected to provide for their families and save when they are required to pay Rs. 420,000 in tax on an annual income of Rs. 2,500,000 above the tax-free threshold of Rs. 1,800,000, and thereafter pay tax at 36%?

Unless we have a fair and justifiable tax regime, the future is going to be bleak for Sri Lanka.

title: Financing Sri Lanka’s post-IMF development | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:45
-     - 7

Although the IMF program ends in March 2027, the framework it installed does not. Austerity has been converted into a legal architecture. Any Government that wishes to finance development after 2027 will find that the fiscal space to do so has been pre-emptively legislated away, and that the debt service profile steps up sharply from 2028 as the restructured Bonds begin to amortise in earnest

By Kasun Kariyawasam and Shiran Illanperuma

In March 2027, Sri Lanka’s Extended Fund Facility with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will expire. It is the seventeenth arrangement the country has entered into with the Fund since 1965. That number is not a footnote; it is the argument. Sixteen previous left the underlying structure of the economy intact – an economy that imports what it consumes, exports what it cannot process further, and borrows to cover the difference. Each program ended, and the conditions that produced it reassembled themselves.

The seventeenth has been the most invasive. Approved on 20 March 2023, in the aftermath of the sovereign default and the uprising that followed, it arrived at a moment of maximum leverage for the creditor and minimum room for the debtor. Fiscal consolidation was achieved primarily through indirect taxation, so that the burden fell heaviest on the poor. Energy subsidies were withdrawn and utility pricing made cost-reflective, transmitting global price movements directly into household budgets and industrial input costs. Public investment was compressed, and public sector wages held below inflation for years. 

The revenue target was met but the social consequences are now well documented.

First, poverty in Sri Lanka roughly doubled after 2022 and has remained near a quarter of the population – a level not seen for two decades. Malnutrition among children, school dropout, and the depletion of household savings and assets are the transmission channels through which a fiscal adjustment becomes a lost generation. 

Second, the most mobile and most skilled workers – nurses, doctors, engineers, IT workers – have left in numbers that constitute a structural loss of productive capacity, subsidised by the Sri Lankan State and captured by the labour markets of the Gulf, East Asia, and the West.

Third, and the least discussed, is the loss of economic sovereignty. The Central Bank Act of 2023 grants the Central Bank of Sri Lanka operational independence under a narrow inflation-targeting mandate and prohibits the monetary financing of Government deficits, removing an instrument of development finance that every industrialised economy used on its way up. The Economic Transformation Act of 2024 legislates the program’s own quantitative targets as binding statutory obligations on all future governments.

Although the IMF program ends in March 2027, the framework it installed does not. Austerity has been converted into a legal architecture. Any Government that wishes to finance development after 2027 will find that the fiscal space to do so has been pre-emptively legislated away, and that the debt service profile steps up sharply from 2028 as the restructured Bonds begin to amortise in earnest.

Instruments on the table

Three instruments are currently under discussion for managing the debt portfolio. Each is worth examining on its merits, and each shares a common limitation.

Macro-linked Bonds: The upside triggers are more likely to be hit than the underlying real economy warrants, because the reference variable is dollar GDP. A nominal appreciation of the rupee lifts dollar GDP without a single additional unit of output being produced. The control variable intended to guard against precisely this – a requirement of 11.5% cumulative real growth – is a low bar following two consecutive years of contraction, when the base effect alone does much of the work. The country may find itself paying creditors a growth premium for an exchange rate movement.

Climate swaps: Debt-for-nature and debt-for-climate arrangements can retire a portion of the stock and may unlock multilateral climate grants, which are concessional. But they do not address the productive structure that generates the deficit in the first place, and their conditionalities – conservation commitments over land, forest, and coastal zones – can cut directly against the industrial and energy build-out that any serious development strategy requires. A country cannot finance debt relief by constraining its own industrialisation.

Bond buybacks: Retiring restructured Bonds converts a contingent, complex portfolio into a plainer one, which makes debt management tractable. If the Bonds trade below face or recovery value, Sri Lanka retires debt at a discount. Lazard reportedly advised this course for Zambia, so the playbook exists. However, Sri Lankan Bonds have performed strongly since the restructuring, which means the discount that would make a buyback attractive has largely disappeared. A buyback becomes cheap only if sentiment softens again, or if specific contingent tranches are marked down on fear of the upside triggers. Moreover, a sovereign buying back its own debt shortly after a restructuring invites the interpretation that it anticipates difficulty, which raises the cost of future issuance. Selective buybacks are worth pursuing, given the uncertain external environment and the value of a cleaner portfolio, but that they are a marginal improvement rather than a solution.

All three instruments manage the existing stock of debt. None of them generates new finance for development. They are exercises in liability management, and a country cannot manage its way out of underdevelopment. Sri Lanka needs relief and it needs capital, and the current conversation addresses only the first.

Building the domestic architecture

New financing without new institutions reproduces the crisis. Before Sri Lanka seeks capital abroad, it must rebuild the machinery that governs how it borrows.

The primary dealer system requires reconstruction on a proper legal footing. Before the crisis, the primary dealer network degenerated into a captive placement channel: when the Central Bank could no longer absorb unsold stock, dealers took paper on terms set by proximity rather than price. This is allocation by moral suasion, and it produced a domestic debt market that told the Government nothing useful about the cost of its own borrowing. Rebuilding it with binding contractual obligations, genuine capital requirements, and published performance rankings – as China does for its own dealer network – would restore price discovery. A Government that cannot read a true yield curve cannot manage a debt portfolio.

Sri Lanka also needs a published Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy (MTDS) with explicit targets for the composition of the portfolio: external against domestic, concessional against commercial, and fixed against floating rate. Borrowing at present is reactive, driven by immediate financing needs rather than by a strategic view of currency, rollover, and interest rate risk. An MTDS makes those trade-offs visible and accountable. It is unglamorous and it is prerequisite.

China angle

Sri Lanka’s most underused financial asset is its existing relationship with China’s monetary and capital market infrastructure. A currency swap line of 10 billion RMB is already in place, renewed in 2025, and it functions almost entirely as a passive reserve backstop. It could be the foundation of a financing strategy.

Broaden the use of RMB for trade settlement. The swap is presently constrained in its permitted uses. Extending it to cover bilateral trade invoicing and settlement would reduce the dollar dependency that is the primary transmission channel for external volatility into the Sri Lankan economy. Every import invoiced in dollars is a claim on reserves that fluctuates with US monetary policy, over which Sri Lanka has no influence whatsoever.

Request eligibility for the FIMA RMB repo facility. China’s facility, announced in June 2026, provides eligible central banks with access to RMB liquidity against holdings of Chinese Government Bonds. For Sri Lanka this would mean an RMB reserve buffer that is genuinely liquid rather than notional, and a second source of emergency liquidity that does not require a Fund program as its precondition.

Issue panda Bonds in the onshore Chinese market. Sri Lanka has already begun refinancing dollar-denominated loans from Chinese banks into RMB, which establishes the precedent and the relationships. Issuance in the Shanghai interbank market would lock in RMB funding at rates below what the Eurobond market will offer a recently defaulted sovereign, and it diversifies the creditor base away from the Paris Club and Western commercial holders whose collective action in 2022 and 2023 was itself a lesson in concentration risk.

Access the offshore dim sum market in Hong Kong. The offshore CNH market is deep – new issuance reached $157.2 billion in 2025 – and is a plausible source of medium-term infrastructure financing on terms that do not carry policy conditionality.

Integrate with CIPS. None of the above scales without payments infrastructure. Integration with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System reduces exposure to dollar-clearing volatility, carries lower transaction costs than routing through SWIFT correspondent banking, and is what allows the swap facilities to be used at volume rather than symbolically.

Establish direct LKR–RMB settlement. Building on the Indonesia–HKMA–PBoC framework of June 2026, a direct settlement mechanism for bilateral trade would give Sri Lanka a working channel into one of the largest markets in the world, and create a pipeline for foreign direct investment and other inflows that does not transit the dollar system at all.

Multipolarity as infrastructure

What Sri Lanka should build is a blueprint for a local currency settlement corridor that can be scaled to any partner. Begin with China, where the infrastructure already exists, and extend it to India, the country’s nearest neighbour and one of its largest trading partners, where rupee settlement arrangements are already operating with other states. The same institutional template – bilateral swap, direct settlement mechanism, payments system linkage, local currency invoicing – applies to any counterparty with which Sri Lanka has meaningful two-way trade.

The immediate prize is energy. A large share of Sri Lankan inflation originates in oil, transmitted through both the world price and the exchange rate at which it is paid. That volatility does not merely raise the cost of living; it creates genuine industrial hurdles, because manufacturers cannot plan around input costs that move with a currency they do not earn. Denominating energy imports in local currency terms would break one of the most damaging transmission channels between external shocks and domestic prices. For a country whose recent history is defined by a fuel queue, this is not an abstraction.

Multipolarity, understood correctly, is a portfolio strategy. A sovereign with settlement channels in several currencies, funding relationships across several capital markets, and reserve buffers denominated in more than one unit of account is a sovereign with options during a crisis. Sri Lanka in 2022 had none, and the terms it accepted in 2023 reflect that.

title: Beyond beaches and heritage: Why Sri Lanka must embrace Muslim-friendly tourism | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:38
-     - 9

Perhaps Sri Lanka’s greatest advantage is its authenticity. The country has a long-established Muslim community, historic mosques and Islamic heritage sites, and a culinary tradition that naturally offers a wide range of halal-friendly food. From Colombo’s historic Islamic quarters to Beruwala, Kandy and other parts of the country, there is an Islamic heritage story waiting to be properly curated and presented to international visitors

Sri Lanka has long been celebrated for its breathtaking landscapes, rich cultural heritage and warm hospitality. Yet, as global tourism evolves, there is another opportunity that the country can no longer afford to overlook: Muslim-friendly tourism.

The global Muslim travel market is among the fastest-growing segments of international tourism. Sri Lanka already has many of the ingredients needed to compete; an established Muslim community, centuries of Islamic heritage, halal culinary traditions, mosques across the country, beautiful beaches, wildlife, wellness and family-oriented experiences. The challenge is not whether Sri Lanka can serve Muslim travellers. It is whether it can do so systematically, consistently and strategically.

According to the latest figures outlined in a strategic proposal for developing Muslim-friendly tourism in Sri Lanka, Muslim visitor arrivals to the country reached 350,858 in 2025, surpassing the previous peak recorded in 2017. Sri Lanka is also ranked 60th in the Global Muslim Travel Index 2025 (GMTI 2025), indicating both an existing presence and considerable room for improvement.

A timely initiative

There are encouraging signs that this opportunity is beginning to receive greater attention.

Marshad Barry, immediate past President of the Sri Lanka–Malaysia Business Council, has recently taken an initiative to promote Muslim-friendly tourism in Sri Lanka, with the support of Malaysia’s Islamic Tourism Centre (ITC). The initiative included an awareness program bringing together academia, tourism industry professionals and policymakers an important first step in creating a common understanding of what Muslim-friendly tourism means and why it matters.

This is significant because Muslim-friendly tourism is not simply about providing halal food or a prayer room. It is about designing a complete visitor experience that takes into account the cultural, religious and service expectations of Muslim travellers.

As the strategic assessment of Sri Lanka’s tourism opportunity highlights, the country’s strengths are considerable from its compact geography and natural attractions to its Islamic heritage and culinary traditions. However, fragmented offerings, inconsistent halal assurance, limited international visibility and gaps in workforce readiness remain important challenges.

Infrastructure alone will not be enough

The global authority on Muslim-friendly travel, ratings, accreditation, GMTI insights and halal tourism strategy, CrescentRating Founder snf CEO Fazal Bahardeen puts the opportunity into perspective: 

“Sri Lanka has real strengths to build on, but capturing its share of a market headed for 262 million Muslim arrivals and $ 310 billion in expenditure by 2030 will take more than infrastructure. The country needs sustained capacity building across the hospitality sector, formal accreditation for hotels and tourism properties, and destination marketing that actively targets high-value Muslim travellers.”

This is an important message for Sri Lanka. The country does not necessarily need to build an entirely new tourism industry. Rather, it needs to upgrade, standardise and strategically market what it already has.

Countries such as Thailand, Hong Kong and Taiwan demonstrate what is possible. Their success in attracting Muslim travellers has not come simply from adding halal restaurants and prayer facilities. They have invested in staff training, service design, Muslim-friendly facilities, digital information and targeted marketing, particularly in Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian source markets.

For Sri Lanka, this is where the real opportunity lies. Muslim travellers from the Gulf, Malaysia, Indonesia and other Asian markets are not simply looking for a hotel room. They are looking for confidence: Can I find halal food? Where can I pray? Will the hotel understand my needs? Can my family enjoy the destination comfortably? Is the information reliable?

From opportunity to policy

There is also growing recognition within Sri Lanka’s academic and policy circles.

University of Colombo Professor of Tourism Economics Prof. (Dr.) D.A.C. Suranga Silva, a member of Sri Lanka’s Tourism Advisory Committee, has already prepared a concept paper outlining how this lucrative segment could be promoted as part of the country’s wider tourism development strategy. He intends to present it to the Advisory Committee.

Such initiatives could help move the discussion beyond isolated projects towards a more coordinated national approach.

Aventra Travels Ltd. Founder/CEO Mafaz Mashood, one of the pioneers in Muslim-friendly tour operations in Sri Lanka, sees the opportunity directly from the marketplace.

He notes that his company has consistently received enquiries from Muslim travellers overseas asking about the availability of Muslim-friendly accommodation, halal food and other services in Sri Lanka. At present, however, many of these arrangements are handled in a fragmented manner.

“I highly recommend that the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority recognise this fast-growing segment and include Muslim-friendly tourism within the national tourism framework of Sri Lanka,” he says.

The demand is not theoretical. Mashood recently concluded a women-only Muslim tour group from Europe, demonstrating that specialised Muslim travel segments are already looking towards Sri Lanka.

Building the ecosystem

The next step should be to create a genuine Muslim-friendly tourism ecosystem, rather than a collection of individual initiatives.

The country’s tourism authorities, hotel associations, tour operators, travel agents and tourist-guide associations all have a role to play. Universities and hotel schools should consider incorporating Muslim-friendly tourism, cultural awareness and service requirements into their tourism and hospitality curricula.

At the industry level, organisations such as the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority, hotel and hospitality associations, tour operators, travel agents and tourist-guide associations should regularly invite specialists in Muslim-friendly tourism to conduct awareness programs for their members.

This is particularly important for frontline employees. A destination can have excellent infrastructure, but one poorly informed staff interaction can undermine the entire visitor experience.

The strategic pathway proposed for Sri Lanka similarly emphasises education, certification, capability building and the development of a credible rating and accreditation framework for hotels, resorts, restaurants and attractions.

Sri Lanka has something others cannot easily replicate

Perhaps Sri Lanka’s greatest advantage is its authenticity.

The country has a long-established Muslim community, historic mosques and Islamic heritage sites, and a culinary tradition that naturally offers a wide range of halal-friendly food. From Colombo’s historic Islamic quarters to Beruwala, Kandy and other parts of the country, there is an Islamic heritage story waiting to be properly curated and presented to international visitors.

This should not mean turning Sri Lanka into a destination exclusively for Muslim travellers. Quite the opposite. Muslim-friendly tourism is about making a destination more inclusive and accessible while retaining its authentic identity.

The same facilities and service improvements; better food information, cleaner prayer spaces, culturally aware staff, family-friendly services and clearer digital information can enhance the experience for many other visitors as well.

The questions Sri Lanka must now ask

The opportunity is clear. But opportunity alone does not create competitiveness.

Are we reaching the right Muslim source markets or are we simply waiting for them to find us?

Are our current tourism strategies effectively addressing the needs of this fast-growing segment?

Are our hotels, restaurants, tour operators, guides and attractions genuinely ready to deliver a consistent Muslim-friendly experience?

And perhaps the most important question:

Will Sri Lanka allow Muslim-friendly tourism to remain a collection of individual efforts or will it have the vision to make it part of the country’s national tourism strategy?

Sri Lanka already possesses many of the ingredients. What it needs now is coordination, standards, skills, confidence and a clear market strategy.

The next chapter of Sri Lankan tourism may not require discovering a new attraction. It may simply require the country to look at its existing strengths through the eyes of a new generation of travellers and make them feel that Sri Lanka was ready to welcome them all along.

(The author is a Global Muslim-Friendly Tourism and Halal Industry consultant. He can be contacted via email: Irshad.cader@globothink.com)

title: The undesirable future | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:30
-     - 8

The art and science of foresight studies has evolved to allow us to develop various perspectives of the future. Combined with the advantages of the information age, foresight studies allow us to essentially wield a “crystal ball” to look around and peer deep into a particular angle of what might be. This is a proven corporate discipline

In the current chaos of geopolitical competition and conflict, the future is not clear. What if I told you we can reasonably estimate where we are heading? 

Imagine the coastal towns of your childhood reduced to skeletal steel structures, abandoned after repeated, unmanaged floods. Once viable communities are now emptied of people and purpose. Rubble piles mark where hotels and guest houses stood before the last hurricane. Broken concrete blocks and twisted metal beams lie scattered where streets once connected neighbors to markets, to work, to life. Fishing communities no longer exist as there are no fish in the once abundant coastal waters. The few remaining structures are boarded up, claimed by no one.

By 2030 compliance systems have collapsed, characterised by discarded social safety nets, dismantled economic safeguards and political coherence dissolved into transactional Environmental regulations, as luxuries no nation can afford, are abandoned. Governments lack the bandwidth to govern. Global agreements unravel into unenforceable disputes. Climate shocks continue relentlessly - floods, fires, droughts, heat waves. There is no coordinated response, only isolated, competing struggles for survival. The green transition never happened, not because we lacked the technology, but because the institutional architecture required to manage a global energy transition has completely broken down. States are too weak. Markets are too fractured. The world fragments into competing fiefdoms, private safe havens, and abandoned regions.

This is a view from “Fragmented Breakdown”, the future scenario where institutional machinery simply ceases to function.

Businesses must assess their readiness to adapt: Can your supply chains function outside protected economic blocs and in the face of global logistical bottlenecks? Do you have redundancy in power, water, and local logistics? Where can you relocate operations if floods or droughts make your current locations unviable? These are not comfortable questions, but they are necessary ones

How to read the future: A foresight primer

Can we truly look into the future? We live in the information age where data is at our fingertips; for example we could obtain fifty years of historical prices for a kilogram of rice in China or for a kilogram of black pepper in Sri Lanka. This could be accomplished using the search engine of choice.

The art and science of foresight studies has evolved to allow us to develop various perspectives of the future. Combined with the advantages of the information age, foresight studies allow us to essentially wield a "crystal ball" to look around and peer deep into a particular angle of what might be. This is a proven corporate discipline; multinational leaders like Shell have used foresight studies and scenario building since the 1970s to guide their strategy. The scenario planning carried out by Shell, enabled them to anticipate oil demand volatility and invest in renewables earlier than competitors. These strategy exercises would have typically been conducted over several weeks with dozens of experts providing inputs in different ways.

Artificial intelligence tools can be leveraged to sift through the ‘noise’ of current data in all its abundance. Unlike in the past, this automated use of established methods enables rapid generation of possible future(s). I say futures in the plural because this methodology is not an all-knowing crystal ball that knows the future with absolute certainty. Foresight studies are methods of identifying how the future can turn out based on what we know now. It identifies driving forces and trends that point toward the extremes that can be reached. These allow us to develop scenarios that essentially outline the borders within which the future can unfold. 

To accurately understand the details of alternative futures, we must first examine the global foundations upon which they depend. To do this, we look at the current baseline and trajectories of environmental systems, politics, demographics, technology, and economic activity.  By analysing large datasets that capture trends across these interconnected systems, we can even apply superforecasting techniques to develop more plausible and discernable pathways to the future. Superforecasting uses historical data and expert analysis to generate more statistically grounded scenarios. For example, our long-term resilience is directly determined by how sustainability is integrated across human activities. Accordingly, exploring the exact nature of technological innovation in energy management can reveal how sustainably we address future energy demand. 

The 2026–2031 Scenario Matrix below, is a set of four distinct future scenarios outlining the global institutional structures that will dictate Sri Lanka's economic and physical resilience.

Future scenarios are interpreted as a cohesive map, not as individual scenarios that are likely to take place. The primary takeaway here is, the time for raising awareness about climate change and environmental stress is gone. We can no longer mitigate the impact of a changing climate. Even if the theory of climate change does not hold, the impacts of repeated destructive climate events and highly stressed global ecosystems are stark. The impacts are too costly to ignore. What we can do is adapt and build resilience. This is a process, not a quick fix. The capacity to adapt to the environmental and climatic realities we will face in the coming years is what will ultimately determine how we survive and thrive or whether we face abandonment and collapse.

Between 2016 and 2025, Sri Lanka experienced multiple extreme weather events, with only Cyclone Ditwah (2025) comprehensively assessed by the World Bank at $4.1 billion in direct physical damage. The total economic loss, including indirect impacts and recovery costs, reaches $6–7 billion, equivalent to 7% of GDP.  This data underscores a critical reality: Sri Lanka's vulnerability to climate shocks is not theoretical. It is measured and documented.

The leaders we elect today will determine whether Sri Lanka builds resilient institutions, invests in distributed infrastructure, and negotiates meaningfully for a place within stable global systems, or whether we drift into abandonment

A Sri Lankan interpretation for the Securitised Integration scenario

According to the Global Climate Risk Index 2025, Sri Lanka ranks among the world's most climate-vulnerable nations, designated in the "red zone" of highest risk in the Asian-Pacific region . This index measures a country's exposure to extreme weather events, floods, cyclones, droughts, and heat waves. In the Securitised Integration scenario, this vulnerability has the potential to become a strategic disadvantage in a divided global economy. 

By 2027, wealthy nations form tight economic blocs and treat climate policy as a national security matter. They re-write trade rules to protect their own supply chains, impose carbon tariffs on outsiders, and restrict access to green technology like advanced battery storage and AI-driven energy systems. Sri Lanka, if excluded from these blocs, faces steep tariffs on its exports of tea, spices, and garments. Export-dependent businesses cannot compete. 

International investors and banks withdraw capital, viewing Sri Lanka as too risky and too far outside the protected economic zones. Capital and financing are not accessible to outsiders. Governments in allied blocs would use state resources and insurance schemes to protect their own industries and economies from climate shocks. Skilled Sri Lankan workers migrate to bloc countries for better opportunities, draining domestic talent and remittances. Climate disasters continue unabated: monsoons flood agricultural land, droughts devastate harvests, and rising seas threaten ports. 

Sri Lanka must adapt alone, without access to affordable capital, protected markets, or international disaster relief. Citizens have little influence over these decisions, they are made by foreign governments and multinational corporations. By 2031, the wealthy blocs have successfully managed their own climate transition. Sri Lanka has fallen further behind, facing intensifying climate shocks with fewer resources and no institutional support.

Reality check

Extremes are needed to understand the scope of what we need to prepare for in the future. The scenarios explore situations that have already been faced on some level, worldwide. While it may take over a decade for these trends to impact on the level depicted by the future scenarios, they give us an opportunity to prepare early.

The foresight process outlined in this article is not prediction—it is context for preparation. Businesses must assess their readiness to adapt: Can your supply chains function outside protected economic blocs and in the face of global logistical bottlenecks? Do you have redundancy in power, water, and local logistics? Where can you relocate operations if floods or droughts make your current locations unviable? These are not comfortable questions, but they are necessary ones.

The responsibility extends beyond boardrooms. Citizens must recognise that these futures are not inevitable, they are a choice. The leaders we elect today will determine whether Sri Lanka builds resilient institutions, invests in distributed infrastructure, and negotiates meaningfully for a place within stable global systems, or whether we drift into abandonment. Patriotism in this moment means voting for leaders with the long-term vision and moral courage to prioritise collective adaptive capacity over short-term political gain. It means demanding transparency and action on climate policy, engaging constructively with environmental impact assessments, and holding the Government accountable for infrastructure investments that protect all Sri Lankans. It means recognising that each of us, in our professional and personal choices, contributes to either resilience or fragility. The time for awareness is over. The time for adaptation is now. The future of Sri Lanka depends on whether we act with the urgency our future demands.

(The author is Vice President at Trident Futures Group, is a Professor of Strategic Security at the Henley-Putnam School of Strategic Security, National American University (USA), and the Co-Editor in Chief of the National Defence College Journal (Sri Lanka)

South Africa came from behind to beat New Zealand 29-24 in a fiercely contested third Test in Soweto on 5 September, 2026, moving 2-1 ahead in the four-match series with one game remaining.

Malcolm Marx’s driving-maul try and a penalty from Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu put the result beyond doubt, with Samisoni Taukei’aho’s late try only a consolation for the visitors.

title: India crush Pakistan at T20 Asia Cup with record-breaking bowling display | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:22

Richa Ghosh of India successfully appeals for the wicket of Shawaal Zulfiqar of Pakistan during the DP World Women’s T20 Asia Cup 2026 match

India on Saturday produced a dominant display to defeat Pakistan by seven wickets in the Women’s T20 Asia Cup in Dubai, bowling their rivals out for their lowest total in the format before rattling off their target inside nine overs.

Pakistan, having won the toss and elected to bat at the Dubai International Stadium on Saturday, made a promising start but collapsed spectacularly after an opening partnership of 27.

India eventually dismissed them for just 55 in 18.1 overs, with their spinners responsible for much of the damage.

Shree Charani and Prema Rawat were the stars of the bowling attack, taking three wickets apiece. Charani finished with remarkable figures of 3 for 7 from four overs, while Rawat returned 3 for 9. Deepti Sharma added two wickets for only five runs.

Pakistan’s innings initially appeared under control. Muneeba Ali made 13, and Shawaal Zulfiqar scored 14 for the first wicket.

But Shafali Verma broke the partnership by bowling Muneeba, and Charani then struck twice in the sixth over. She dismissed Gull Feroza for a duck before removing Zulfiqar, leaving Pakistan 29 for three.

The collapse continued almost immediately as Pakistan slipped to 32 for four in the eighth over before Rawat and Deepti Sharma intensified the pressure. By the 13th over, Pakistan were 45 for seven, and there was no prospect of recovering to a competitive total.

The final three wickets eventually fell with Pakistan on 55, giving India an exceptionally modest target. The total was Pakistan’s lowest in women’s T20I cricket, surpassing their previous low of 63 against India in the 2012 Women’s Twenty20 Asia Cup.

Despite requiring only 56, India did not have everything their own way at the start of the chase.

Pakistan’s bowlers claimed three wickets, giving their opponents a brief glimpse of an unlikely route back into the contest. Fatima Sana was Pakistan’s most successful bowler, finishing with 3 for 17.

The target, however, was simply too small. India reached 57 for three in 8.4 overs, completing a seven-wicket victory with Harmanpreet Kaur unbeaten on 18. The Indian captain ensured there was no late drama and guided her side across the line with plenty of deliveries to spare.

The victory maintained India’s perfect start to the tournament. They now have six points from three matches and have already secured their place in the semifinals.

For Pakistan, meanwhile, the defeat leaves their qualification hopes dependent on their final group match against Hong Kong. They remain on two points and need a victory to give themselves a chance of progressing.

title: Making Sri Lankan sport truly inclusive: From participation to belonging | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:11
-     - 5

If Sri Lanka can create a sporting system where a child with a disability, a girl from a rural school, a child from a low-income family or a young person from any community can see a genuine pathway to participation and excellence, then sport will have achieved something far greater than winning medals

Sport has always been described as a great unifier. It brings together people across ethnic, religious, social and economic boundaries and gives communities a common identity. Yet, if Sri Lanka is serious about using sport as a force for social inclusion, it must ask a difficult question: Are we really making sport accessible to everyone, or are we simply celebrating inclusion when an athlete succeeds?

Sri Lanka has produced outstanding athletes with disabilities, women champions and talented sportspeople from disadvantaged communities. But inclusion cannot be measured only by medals. It must be measured by how many children get an opportunity to play, how many girls remain in sport, how accessible our stadiums are, and whether a child with a disability feels that the sporting field belongs to them too.

Sri Lanka's National Sports Policy already recognises the importance of bringing persons with disabilities into sport and calls on sports bodies to establish mechanisms to integrate them into mainstream activities. The challenge is turning that policy intention into everyday reality.

Move beyond separate competitions

Sri Lanka has made considerable progress in creating opportunities for athletes with disabilities, particularly through Paralympic sport. However, true inclusion should begin long before an athlete reaches the national or international level.

The problem is that many children with disabilities encounter exclusion at the very first stage of participation. School sports programs are often designed around conventional physical abilities, leaving children with disabilities watching from the sidelines. This creates the perception that sport is something they can only participate in through a separate system.

That mindset needs to change.

Schools should introduce inclusive sporting activities in which children of different abilities participate together wherever possible. Athletics, swimming, table tennis, badminton, wheelchair racing, sitting volleyball and adapted versions of traditional games can provide opportunities for everyone.

The objective is not necessarily to make every event identical. Inclusion means creating an equal opportunity to participate, even when the method of participation is different.

Sri Lanka could introduce an annual National Inclusive School Sports Festival, with every province conducting preliminary competitions. Such a program would allow children with disabilities to compete, meet other children and, importantly, be recognised as athletes rather than simply as children requiring assistance.

Make schools the starting point

If Sri Lanka wants a long-term change in sporting culture, schools are the most important starting point.

Schools are where children first develop their attitudes towards competition, teamwork, winning and losing. They are also where children learn whether differences should be respected or treated as barriers.

Unfortunately, many schools still lack trained physical education teachers, adapted equipment and accessible facilities. A child who uses a wheelchair, for example, may technically be allowed to participate but still be unable to reach the playing area.

The Education Ministry, Ministry of Sports, provincial authorities and national federations should therefore develop an Inclusive Physical Education Program.

Physical education teachers should receive basic training in adapting sports for children with different abilities. Schools should also receive simple equipment packages rather than expensive specialised infrastructure in the first stage.

More importantly, inclusion should become part of the school sports culture.

A school sports meet should not merely celebrate the fastest runner or highest jumper. It should celebrate participation, teamwork, perseverance and achievement across different abilities.

Are we really making sport accessible to everyone, or are we simply celebrating inclusion when an athlete succeeds?

Inclusion must also mean gender equality

Sri Lanka has produced outstanding women athletes, yet women's participation in sport continues to face cultural, financial and institutional barriers.

Girls in some communities are still discouraged from participating in sport because of traditional attitudes, concerns about safety, lack of facilities or the belief that sporting careers are unsuitable for women.

This is where schools and communities can make a major difference.

Girls should have access to the same coaching, playing facilities and competitions available to boys. Women's teams should receive proper development programs rather than being formed only when an international tournament approaches.

The problem also extends to leadership.

Sri Lanka needs more women coaches, referees, administrators, technical officials and decision-makers. If young girls never see women sitting on sports boards, coaching national teams or managing major sporting organisations, they may believe that leadership in sport is reserved for men.

Corporate sponsorship can play an important role. Companies could establish long-term programs specifically supporting girls' sport, women's leagues and female coaches.

The objective should be to create a sporting pathway that begins with a girl kicking a ball or picking up a netball and can ultimately take her to the national team, coaching bench or sports administration.

Take sport beyond Colombo

One of Sri Lanka's biggest sporting problems is the concentration of opportunities in Colombo and a few major cities. Talent exists throughout the country, but opportunity does not.

A child in Jaffna, Batticaloa, Anuradhapura, Badulla, Monaragala or Hambantota should have access to quality coaching and competition without having to move to Colombo.

Sri Lanka could establish District Inclusive Sports Centres by using existing government schools, provincial sports complexes and public playgrounds. These need not be expensive high-tech facilities. What is required is proper coordination.

Each district could identify coaches, physical education teachers and volunteers who can conduct regular programs for children with disabilities, girls and children from disadvantaged communities.

This would also create a better talent-identification system.

At present, Sri Lanka may be losing talented athletes simply because nobody discovers them. A national inclusive sports network could create a pathway from village → school → district → province → national level.

Stadiums must belong to everyone

Physical accessibility is one of the most overlooked areas of Sri Lankan sport.

A modern stadium may have excellent floodlights, seating and playing surfaces, but if a wheelchair user cannot enter the venue independently, the facility cannot genuinely be described as inclusive.

Accessibility should become a mandatory requirement for all new sports infrastructure.

Existing stadiums should undergo accessibility audits covering ramps, elevators, toilets, parking, seating, changing rooms and spectator movement.

But accessibility should not be limited to athletes.

A parent with a disability should be able to watch their child compete. An elderly spectator should be able to reach their seat safely. A visually impaired supporter should be able to receive assistance and information.

Sport is not only about the person on the field. It is also about creating an environment in which everyone can participate as a spectator, volunteer, official, coach or supporter.

The media can change the narrative

The media has perhaps the greatest power to change public attitudes towards inclusion.

Too often, para-athletes are covered only when they win medals. Even then, stories sometimes focus more on their disability and personal hardship than on their sporting performance.

That approach should change.

A para-athlete who breaks a national record should receive the same serious sporting analysis as any other athlete. Journalists should discuss technique, preparation, competition, rankings and performance.

The same applies to women's sport.

If newspapers, television channels and digital platforms provide consistent coverage of women's competitions, public interest will grow. Increased public interest will attract sponsors, which will provide better financial resources, which will improve the quality of competition.

It becomes a cycle.

Sri Lankan sports media can therefore become an important partner in building an inclusive sporting culture rather than simply reporting results.

Business has a role too

The private sector should not view inclusion as merely a corporate social responsibility exercise.

It can become a long-term investment in Sri Lankan sport.

Instead of sponsoring only high-profile national teams, companies could adopt schools, districts, women's teams or para-athletes.

For example, a corporate sponsor could fund an inclusive sports program in one district for three years. The program could provide equipment, coaching, transportation and competitions.

Another company would sponsor a group of promising para-athletes, covering training, travel and equipment.

Such programs would give companies measurable social impact while creating stronger relationships with communities.

Sri Lankan businesses already spend considerable amounts on advertising through sport. A portion of that investment could be redirected towards building the next generation of athletes.

Inclusion means creating an equal opportunity to participate, even when the method of participation is different

Inclusion must become a national sporting culture

Ultimately, inclusion cannot be achieved through one government program, one sports federation or one annual event.

It requires a change in culture.

The question should no longer be, “Can this person participate in sport?”

The question should be, “What can we change so that this person can participate?”

That difference in thinking is fundamental.

Sri Lanka has repeatedly demonstrated that when an athlete receives the right opportunity, extraordinary things can happen. The country has produced champions from rural villages, women who have competed against the world's best and para-athletes who have carried the national flag with distinction.

The next challenge is to ensure that these success stories are not exceptions.

Inclusive sport should not be a charity. It should be a right, an investment and a national priority.

If Sri Lanka can create a sporting system where a child with a disability, a girl from a rural school, a child from a low-income family or a young person from any community can see a genuine pathway to participation and excellence, then sport will have achieved something far greater than winning medals.

It will have helped build a more equal Sri Lanka.

title: Betis beat Real Madrid as Mbappe misses penalty in first La Liga defeat | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 03:07
-     - 4

Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe looks dejected after his penalty is saved by Real Betis’s Alvaro Valles on Friday

Kylian Mbappe missed a late penalty as Troy Parrott scored his first goal for Real Betis in a 1-0 win over Real Madrid, ending manager Jose Mourinho’s side’s perfect start to the La Liga season.

Madrid had won each of their first three matches under Mourinho in his second spell in charge, but Betis goalkeeper Alvaro Valles denied Mbappe from the spot deep into stoppage time on Friday to seal a memorable victory at La Cartuja.

Vinicius Junior hit the post in the first half from Arda Guler’s pass across the face of goal, with Mbappe foiled twice by heroic blocks from Natan Bernardo de Souza and Marc Bartra.

As Madrid struggled to break Betis down, the hosts took a surprise lead nine minutes from time when Parrott fired home the rebound after Thibaut Courtois had produced a fine save to deny Nelson Deossa’s header.

Carlos Espi thought he had equalised with a superb acrobatic finish from a Vinicius cross, but the goal was ruled out for offside in the build-up.

Mbappe then clipped the crossbar with a delicate effort before being handed a glorious chance to level from the penalty spot after Natan’s crunching late challenge on Vinicius.

However, Valles saved his kick to secure a victory that lifted Betis level with Madrid on nine points from four matches ahead of just their second Champions League campaign next week.
